title: Is a German Harbour Porpoise much more sensitive than a British one? Comparative analyses of mandatory measures for the protection of Harbour Porposes (Phocoena phocoena) during Offshore Wind Farm ramming in Germany, Denmark and the UK

## **UW109.   Is a German Harbour Porpoise much more sensitive than a British one? Comparative analyses of mandatory measures for the protection of Harbour Porposes (Phocoena phocoena) during Offshore Wind Farm ramming in Germany, Denmark and the UK**

## **Jens Luedeke***

## ***Corresponding author’s address: Technical University of Berlin, Berlin, 10623 Berlin, Berlin, Germany, jens.luedeke@bmu.bund.de**

Offshore wind farms (OWF) will soon contribute to significant growth in the renewable energy sector. At present just a few OWF have been built. As of 2012, Germany has an offshore wind capacity of little more than 200 MW, whereas Denmark has already reached 875 MW and the UK soon will reach 2.000 MW. There are plans for another 114 GW in EU countries, with a cumulative investment of 211 billion Euro. This expansion of offshore wind energy needs to be organized in a sustainable way. The Habitat Directive has to be considered in each European country in the same way. Currently, the environmental impacts of the underwater noise on porpoises, caused by jack-hammers that are mostly used to drive the pile foundations into the seabed, are assessed differently amongst the forerunners of offshore wind energy like Denmark, Great Britain, and Germany. This paper includes an overview of the possible applied measures for avoiding damages, as well as obligatory measures and the different thresholds of European countries. The analysis concludes by identifying a need for international standardization. The paper is result of research as part of the PhD thesis "Strategies for Sustainable Development of Offshore Wind Energy" of the author.

Published by the Acoustical Society of America through the American Institute of Physics

## **Introduction**

Offshore wind farms (OWF) will soon contribute to significant growth in the renewable energy sector. At present just a few OWF have been built. As of 2012, Germany has an offshore wind capacity of little more than 200 MW, whereas Denmark has already reached 875 MW and the UK soon will reach 2,000 MW. Worldwide, the current capacity of installed offshore wind energy is more than 4 GW; 6 GW are currently under construction, and a further 17 GW are consented. All in all there are plans for another 114 GW in EU countries, with a cumulative investment of 211 billion Euros through 2030 (EWEA 2011).

This expansion of offshore wind energy needs to be organized in a sustainable way. The Habitat Directive has to be considered in each European country in the same way. Currently, the environmental impacts of the underwater noise on porpoises, caused by jack-hammers that are mostly used to drive the pile foundations into the seabed, are assessed differently amongst the forerunners of offshore wind energy like Denmark, Great Britain, and Germany. This paper includes an overview of the possible applied measures for avoiding damages, as well as obligatory measures and the different thresholds of European countries. The analysis concludes by identifying a need for international standardization. The paper is result of research as part of the PhD thesis “Strategies for Sustainable Development of Offshore Wind Energy” of the author, contains proposals for the further development of offshore wind energy as an outcome of the research and surely can not be seen as an official statement of Federal Ministry of Environment.

## **1. Legal Background for Protection of the Harbour Porpoise**

Harbour Porpoises are considered an endangered species and are listed in Annexes II and IV of the EU Habitat Directive. European countries are obliged to report natural habitat areas of harbour porpoises to the European Commission (Natura 2000 Sites according to Article 6 of the Habitat Directive) as well as measures for protecting the animals outside of these areas (Article 12 of the Habitat Directive). European Environmental Directives must be considered during the planning process for offshore wind farm projects.[1]

In Germany, large parts of the marine area were announced as Natura 2000 sites, with inter alia the Harbour Porpoise as a protection goal (Krause and v. Nordheim 2008). The populations of the Harbour Porpoise in Denmark and the UK are comparable to that of Germany, and Natura 2000 sites have been established in a comparable way. But the share of Natura 2000 sites in Denmark is much lower. Denmark has only 18,541km2 of protected ocean area, while the UK has protected 36,791 km2 of its marine area (EU COM 2011). In Germany 10,377 km2 of the EEZ (31.5 %) is under protection.

According to the Habitat Directive, the Harbour Porpoise needs to be protected against underwater noise. In terms of the ramming of turbines, significant effects from the noise of ramming (e.g.  killing of animals) on Natura 2000 sites and the site's conservation objectives (e.g. Harbour Porpoises) must be

>

prevented. Next to the killing of animals, it has not yet been clearly shown what durations of disturbances can be seen as thresholds of significant impact for Natura 2000 sites. Generally, most European Countries do not prohibit OWF developments inside Natura 2000 sites (see 4.2). The licensing procedure of an offshore wind farm must prove that marine mammals were neither killed, nor injured by permanent damage to their hearing (Permanent Threshold Shift), inside or outside of Natura 2000 Sites. However, whether an offshore wind farm development has had a direct, injurious impact on marine mammals is not easy to show.

## **2. Negative Effects of Underwater Noise on Marine Mammals**

## **(especially Harbour Porpoises)**

The negative effects of underwater noise from the ramming of offshore wind turbines have been wellknown for years, and are shown by different authors in several compendiums (Hildebrand 2006, Madsen et al. 2006, Parvin et al. 2006a and 2006b, Thomsen et al. 2006, Nowacek et al. 2007, Southall et al. 2007, Weilgart 2007, Nehls et al. 2009, André et al. 2009, Ainslie et al. 2009).

But it is scientifically unclear and there is no consensus, at what point an impairment of the hearing is considered an injury. A temporary threshold shift (TTS) can not yet be physically ascertained, but mainly depends on whether hearing is damaged permanently (PTS) or only limited for a short time. The danger of an injury depends on a variety of factors, including energy content, peak pressure, and signal duration or frequency (Richardson et al 1995). In most cases the TTS seems to be reversible (Nachtigall et al. 2003). So it discussed, if TTS is an adequate advice for an injury as described in Art. 12 of the Habitat Directive. In Germany the threshold of 160 dB SEL is based on the TTS. Standardized models should be established to help answer these questions (Nehls and Betke 2011, Nehls et al 2009).

In most international studies, only a PTS is seen as an injury. Still, it should be avoided, for when marine mammals are disturbed by the noise, the continuance of the local population is endangered. This could happen if, for example, reproduction can not take place. The disturbances of the ramming are monitored at a range of 8 to 20 km (without avoidance measures). But it cannot yet be proven that such a disturbance can have any effect on the population. In latest investigation of the ramming process in the offshore wind farm Borkum West II, Nehls 2012 has shown, that disturbance effects with the use of a bubble curtain seem to be much lower than expected. At a range between 7 and 10 km from the construction site, the majority of the harbour porpoise seem to stay in the area and no effects on the harbour porpoises could be shown. But these results still have to be proven statistically (Nehls 2012).

Recent international research affirmed the negative effects of underwater noise on mammals, but did not reach a clear answer as to thresholds for killing or disturbance that would be suitable for the licensing process (Lucke et al. 2011 and 2011a, Michael et al 2010, Baleya et al 2010, Thompson et

al. 2010, Finneran et al. 2010, Doman and Simmonds 2010, Wright et al 2010, Simmonds et al 2010, Diederichs et al 2011, Wilson et al 2010, Kastelein et al 2011).

## **3. Technical Measures for Neutralizing or Avoidance of Underwater**

## **Noise of the Ramming of Offshore Wind Farms**

Scientists have tried to deal with the problem of the possible damage to mammals’ hearing caused by underwater noise. There is an existing body of research, in particular with regard to minimizing the noise by air-bubbles in the water (ISD et al 2007; Nehls et al 2007 and 2009; Grießmann et al 2010a; Koschinsky & Lüdemann 2011).

## **3.1 Acoustic Mitigation (AMD) and Acoustic Harassment (AHD) Devices**

In Germany, Hoeschle et al. 2010 tested the effects of an acoustic harassment device (AHD) on the behaviour of Harbour Porpoises, for deterring Porpoises from entering the zone where there is danger of harmful noise. The results showed that AHDs can substantially help to exclude porpoises from the area of harmful noise.

In addition, Kastelein et al. 2010 tried to avoid damages from underwater noise to marine mammals by means of safe sound from Acoustic Mitigation Devices (AMDs). They estimated the range in which these AMDs were working and showed the distance of any behavioural responses to the AMD. These results are promising as well.

## **3.2 State of the Art of Mitigation Measures of Underwater Noise Caused by**

## **Ramming**

Outside of the well-known “Bubble Curtains” (Koschinsky und Lüdemann 2011, Lucke et al 2011, Grießmann et al 2010, Nehls 2011), pile sleeves can also be a method for minimizing underwater noise. IHC Noise Mitigation Screens have great potential for mitigation (> 20 dB). But an ESRA test in the Baltic Sea has shown that they have not yet reached this high potential. The other different mitigation measures (e.g. BEKA Jacket, Ring of Fire Hoses, Cofferdam, Hydro Sound Dampers) that were examined in the ESRA test there have yet fulfilled the hoped for reductions, of about 20 dB or even more, achieved in the design models. So more scientific research is required to achieve that goal (Offshore Stiftung 2011). A test at the newest German offshore wind farm Riffgat with the Noise mitigation Screen and in Borkum II with the Big Bubble Curtain as well as the Little Bubble Curtain in the offshore windfarm BARD I showed promising results. Still recent tests in 2012 in UK of the Hydro Sound Damper (London Array) and in Denmark of the Cofferdam (Aarhus) were successful in the mitigation of the sound.

## **4. International Comparison of Measures of Avoidance and**

## **Threshold Setting**

In order to determine suitable protective measures for species and habitat protection from noise emissions due to wind farm construction, the author surveyed five recognized experts from each of the three leading countries in offshore wind energy: Germany, the United Kingdom, and Denmark. A questionnaire was sent which was always supplemented by personal or telephonic interviews. The results of the survey have been complemented by a literature review.

The questionnaire, which referred to the regulation in the respective countries, included questions on mitigation, monitoring, and habitat protection. It asked for the different obligatory measures of avoidance necessary in Germany, the UK, and Denmark. Mitigation strategies for avoiding the impacts of noise emissions on marine mammals can be divided between emission reduction measures (like bubble curtains or binding thresholds) and measures that reduce the impacts on a specific receptor. For example, to reduce the impacts on Harbour Porpoises, measures which pause or stop construction work at sensible periods, or avoid cumulative impacts in a specific area, are discussed. Other strategies are focused on deterrent effects by slowly increasing noise emissions from construction in order to displace impacted species.

A very important aspect for improving mitigation measures, and, additionally, for specifying the impacts of noise emissions on marine mammals, is to implement a monitoring system. In terms of habitat protection, noise emissions are a controversial subject. Some countries prefer marine protected areas (MPA) as a ‘recreation zone’ for marine mammals, including a buffer zone that prohibits offshore wind parks adjacent to MPAs. Others allow wind parks in MPAs since they can coexist without compromising the protection regime.

However, as mentioned before, each country has established different mitigation strategies. In this section, three examples are presented in order to propose an international standard for noise mitigation from construction of offshore wind energy facilities.

## **4.1 Germany**

Germany tried to avoid sensitive areas for mammals by implementing spatial planning with suitable areas for OWF. This spatial planning effort did not completely reach its aim, as it did not manage to prevent OWF outside of those suitability areas (Luedeke and Koeppel 2010) The leading authority for approvals, the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH), requires the construction company to apply the best available techniques for avoiding impacts on marine mammals. These measures include, among others deterrent techniques: A pinger used 30 minutes before pile driving and a seal scarer started 20 minutes before pile driving. Bubble curtains have recently been tested and may be implemented during construction over the next several years. Additionally, defined construction periods are discussed intensively in order to reduce cumulative noise emissions which might result in displacements of marine mammals in large areas. Furthermore, for four years the approval of offshore

wind parks includes a binding threshold for noise emissions of 160 dB SEL at a distance of 750m from the construction area. This value is criticized by experts, as it is a ‘rule of thumb’ without sufficient scientific basis. It considers only one drive and neither the periodic noise emissions during the hammering of the piles, nor the species specific channel for acoustic signals. Marine protected areas are really not open for wind energy development, as the Renewable Energy Law does not offer the feed-in tariff, if the wind farm is planned inside a Natura 2000 site. Additionally, two OWF inside Natura 2000 sites in the Baltic Sea have already been rejected for environmental reasons.

## **4.2. United Kingdom**

In the United Kingdom, the leading authorities for approving OWF have not implemented any thresholds or obligatory noise reduction measures. The Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC 2009) is in doubt about the relevance of under water noise emissions during construction work for marine mammals. Thus, they do not propose measures for avoiding or reducing noise emissions. The cost and effort to realize them are too large in comparison to the benefits. This 2009 evaluation is based on the method of Nedwell et al. 2003, which specifies that impacts on Harbour Porpoises are mainly expected near the construction site. The resulting target values are not obligatory for approval. However, to reduce the impacts of construction work, the leading authorities in the UK require the application of deterrent methods in combination with construction monitoring by experts. In the UK, it is permitted to build OWF inside marine protected areas (MPA), after having undertaken an appropriate assessment. Currently more binding thresholds and mitigation measures are under discussion in UK.

## **4.3. Denmark**

Comparable to the UK, the approving authority in Denmark does not require measures for reducing noise emissions (e.g. bubble curtains or other methods). In their opinion, deterrent methods are sufficient to reduce the impacts on specific species to an acceptable level. Hence, there was no need to define a threshold like in Germany. Additionally, cumulative effects have not been considered up to now, as wind farm projects have been realized without spatial relation to each other. Generally, monitoring is not obligatory. However, an extensive monitoring programme of large-scale OWF has, over a seven year period with a BACI (Before-After-Control-Impact) design, measured the impacts on porpoises of two different OWF – one in the Baltic Sea and one in the North Sea (Horns Rev and Nysted). The result of this programme, as well as the results of both similar programmes and follow up programmes, has not created a case for general concern. Thus, it will always be a case specific assessment as to whether or not monitoring is deemed necessary. In Denmark, Marine protected areas are (as in the UK) open for wind energy development, but, of course, an appropriate assessment is necessary. On the basis of a concrete evaluation in the context of the Environmental Impact Assessment and Appropriate Assessment of the effects of the relevant wind farm, one small scale OWF (seven turbines on gravity foundations) has been built in a Natura 2000 area. But the construction of the wind farm had to be outside the breeding season of porpoises and had to be erected on gravity foundations. A monitoring programme was put in place. However, large-scale OWF must be placed outside Natura 2000 areas.

Obviously all three countries have some kind of a monitoring for the effect on mammals and try to minimize the risk of injury by soft start method. There are also forms of deterrence attempted, in different ways, in each country. The only country making use of all the other methods is Germany, which has noise thresholds, obligatory noise reduction methods, and a prohibition of the construction of OWF inside marine protected areas. In none of the countries was there a time where ramming of offshore turbines was forbidden in order to protect mammals, but the idea has been discussed in Germany and remains an issue of debate. Nearly all experts desired some move towards international standards. Most of the experts (>80%), called for international standards for acoustic monitoring/observers while pile driving, for soft start, for obligatory noise reduction measures, for the prohibition of wind farms within MPA, and for methods of deterrence before ramming (seal scarer, pinger).

However, the experts were not as explicit in their desire for standards in the field of thresholds and periods for the exclusion of ramming. Especially the Danish and British experts did not have a clear position on standards in that area. When the experts were asked at what level all these special standards should be established (higher or lower as in their home countries) no clear evidence was provided in any of the different answers of the experts.

## **5. Conclusion and Discussion**

It can be summarized that the three examined countries have very different approaches to dealing with the problem of underwater noise from the ramming sound produced when installing OWF. It seems obvious that an international standard would help define the best way to consider, on the one hand, the European regulations for species protection and to reach, on the other hand, the ambitious goals for offshore wind energy. As the mammals do not stay within each country’s national water zones, they should not be seen as a national subject of protection, but rather as an international issue. Furthermore, OWF should be assessed in an internationally standardized way in order to accurately estimate cumulative effects on the international population levels of mammals.

Therefore, the formation of an international working group would allow for the sharing of experiences from, and the results of scientific efforts in, the different countries. One attempt for such an exchange between different European countries has already been made by the Joint Declaration on Cooperation in the Field of Research on Offshore Wind Energy Deployment. This cooperation should be strengthened, and international research projects should be supported in order to develop international standards on a European level.

Sharing data and experiences relevant for Offshore Wind Energy Deployment on the interaction of the marine environment and ecosystems with technical systems in the European Seas should also be institutionalised internationally. Ultimately, standards for the protection of marine mammals from underwater noise need to be established on a European level.  Such international standards would pave the way to a Europe-wide solution for establishing OWF that would prevent the endangerment of “international mammals”.
